newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: ZIMBABWE CARGO CARRIER SAYS STAYING AIRBORNE.
newsitem.headline: ZIMBABWE CARGO CARRIER SAYS STAYING AIRBORNE.

text.p: Zimbabwe's state-owned national cargo airline looks set to stay airborne despite financial and operational woes as well as increased competition in the industry, an official said on Friday.

"Affretair has always maintained that it is not afraid of competition and in this regard, despite the arrival of other airlines, Affretair has been able to maintain its market share whilst the competition has acquired its business from the market growth," said Affretair sales manager Phil Critchlow.

The latest figures available from the Horticultural Promotion Council show that despite the arrival of some 15 additional carriers offering services to that industry and breaking a monopoly formerly held by Affretair, the state cargo carrier still maintains the top notch in export volumes.
Affretair accounted for 308.5 tonnes of flowers exported in February with Air Zimbabwe following with 151.3 tonnes.
Critchlow said the airline had remained competitive by tailoring its pricing and destinations to market demands.
"This is proved by the fact that Affretair had no spare capacity during the flower season," she told Reuters.

Earlier this month, transport and energy minister Simon Moyo said the national cargo airline was facing financial and operational problems which had put off potential investors interested in taking equity in the company.
He cited shortage of equipment as one of the factors contributing to the inefficiency of the airline.

But Critchlow said the airline's subcontracting policy had enabled the company to maintain a positive perfomance in the last 12 months, despite the increasing age of its DC8 55F aircraft which restricted capacity and operational flexibility, especially in Europe where such aircraft were being phased out.
Affretair was currently operating the DC8 55F freighter and a leased DC10 30F freighter with a total capacity per week of 165 tonnes.
By September or October this year it hopes to have its own wide-body aircraft in operation to replace the leased plane.
It then plans to increase its weekly flights to four from three to accommodate the increase in export tonnages at the peak of the horticulture marketing season which starts in July.
